title: Citizen science
explanation: Compare your response with the model. Preserve the main information and check the task requirements.
audioText: Citizen science allows members of the public to contribute to scientific research. A familiar example is a bird survey in which volunteers record the species they see in their gardens. Because researchers cannot visit every location themselves, these observations can reveal patterns across a much larger area. However, collecting many observations is not enough on its own. Volunteers need clear instructions so that their records can be compared. Researchers may also ask participants to submit photographs, which help specialists check unusual sightings. Another challenge is that some places attract far more volunteers than others. A city park may be surveyed every week while a remote forest receives little attention. For that reason, researchers must consider where observations came from before drawing conclusions. When these limitations are understood, citizen science can both expand the evidence available to scientists and help communities learn about their environment.
model: Public volunteers expand research coverage, but clear instructions, verification and attention to uneven sampling are necessary.

title: Retrieval practice
explanation: Compare your response with the model. Preserve the main information and check the task requirements.
audioText: Many students prepare for examinations by rereading their notes. This feels productive because the information becomes familiar. Familiarity, however, is not the same as being able to recall an idea without help. Retrieval practice involves closing the book and trying to explain what you remember. A student might answer a short question, draw a diagram from memory or teach the concept to a friend. The attempt can reveal gaps that rereading hides. Importantly, checking the answer afterwards is part of the process, because practising an error repeatedly is unlikely to help. Researchers also distinguish a difficult attempt from an impossible one. Questions should require effort while remaining connected to material that the learner has studied. Spacing these attempts across several days can support longer retention than completing them all in one session. The practical lesson is to combine review with opportunities to retrieve information and correct misunderstandings.
model: Retrieval reveals gaps hidden by rereading. Use achievable questions, corrective feedback and spaced practice.

title: Community gardens
explanation: Compare your response with the model. Preserve the main information and check the task requirements.
text: Community gardens are often promoted as a way to grow fresh food, but their social value may be just as important. Residents who previously had little contact can meet while caring for shared plots. Experienced gardeners pass on practical knowledge, and newcomers gain an informal reason to spend time outdoors. These benefits do not arise automatically. A garden that has no clear arrangements for watering, tool storage or access may become a source of disagreement. Some communities address this problem by agreeing on simple rules at the start and reviewing them each season. Others appoint a coordinator to make sure tasks are shared fairly. Successful gardens therefore depend on social organization as well as suitable soil and sunlight. Their value lies in the combination of food production, cooperation and opportunities for local residents to learn from one another.
model: Community gardens can produce food and strengthen local relationships, but they need fair responsibilities and clear rules to turn a shared growing space into a lasting community resource.

title: Digital archives
explanation: Compare your response with the model. Preserve the main information and check the task requirements.
text: Digitizing historical documents can make them available to readers who cannot travel to an archive. High-quality images also reduce the need to handle fragile originals. Yet the process involves more than photographing pages. Each item needs a description that helps readers discover it, and the files must be stored in formats that future systems can open. Handwritten words may be difficult for automated recognition software to interpret, so a searchable version often requires human checking. There are also choices about which records to digitize first. Popular collections may attract attention while less familiar material remains inaccessible. For these reasons, a digital archive should be understood as a carefully maintained selection rather than a complete replacement for a physical collection. Long-term access depends on continued investment in description, preservation and thoughtful decisions about whose histories are represented.
model: Digital archives widen access and protect fragile documents, but reliable discovery and long-term preservation require accurate descriptions, human checking and careful selection of the records included.

title: Cooler roofs
explanation: This 54-word model captures the mechanism, limitation and need for local evaluation. Other accurate 50–70 word summaries are valid.
audioText: Today I want to discuss why cities are experimenting with cooler roofs. A conventional dark roof absorbs much of the sunlight that reaches it, which can increase the temperature inside a building. A pale roof reflects more sunlight and may reduce the need for air conditioning during hot weather. However, it would be misleading to say that one roof design works equally well everywhere. In a cold region, reflecting winter sunlight could increase heating needs. The material also matters because dust and weathering can reduce its reflectivity over time. Some local governments are testing several surfaces before recommending a particular approach. They measure indoor temperatures, energy use and maintenance costs across different seasons. The main lesson is that a promising technology still needs to be evaluated in context. A cooler roof can be useful, but its overall benefit depends on climate, building design and how well the surface is maintained.

However, their benefits vary with climate, building design and maintenance, and they may increase heating needs in colder regions. Cities are therefore testing materials across seasons, comparing temperatures, energy consumption and costs before recommending solutions suitable for local conditions.
